title: Getting home for less
description: The journey home is a fixed feature of student life, and its price varies wildly depending on when and how you book. A little planning halves it.

body.heading: Book the calendar, not the mood
paragraphs: Train and coach prices generally rise as departure approaches and as popular times sell. The cheapest tickets belong to people who book when term dates are announced — which is to say, early, calmly, and for the less fashionable departure times.

If your route offers advance fares, railcards, or student coach discounts, the savings stack: a discount card that costs a little can pay for itself in a single holiday journey and keep saving all year. Do the maths on your actual route before buying one.

body.heading: Flexibility is a currency
paragraphs: Travelling a day earlier, an hour later, or from the next station along can change the price dramatically. Splitting a journey into separate tickets for each leg is sometimes cheaper than the through ticket — price-comparison sites will often check this for you.
Off-peak is your friend. If your timetable allows a mid-morning Tuesday departure instead of the Friday evening rush, the same seat can cost a fraction as much.

body.heading: Share and pool
paragraphs: If friends travel the same route, group discounts, shared taxis for the awkward last leg, or a lift rota with families can cut costs for everyone. And keep a small travel sinking fund during term — a few pounds or dollars a week — so the journey home never competes with the last week of term.

Finally, protect the booking once made: note the ticket's conditions. The cheapest advance tickets are often non-refundable and tied to a specific train, so set alarms and guard the departure time like an exam — a missed cheap ticket is the dearest of all.

takeaway: Book early, travel off-peak, use student and advance discounts, and save a little weekly for the fare — the trip home should cost planning, not panic.
